traits: Turf lifts like loose carpet — roots are gone
White, C-shaped grub with a brown head, in the top few inches of soil
In June beetle (Phyllophaga) grubs, two parallel rows of spines under the tail tip; other scarab grubs show different spine patterns
Armadillos, raccoons, and birds digging at night for an easy meal

look_alikes.difference: White grubs are pale, C-shaped larvae found in soil; June beetles (their adult stage) are brown, oval, hard-shelled beetles that fly at night.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the specimen — a soft C-shaped grub versus a hard-shelled flying beetle.

copy.what_it_means: Animal digging in the lawn at night often points to grubs feeding on roots underneath, but digging alone doesn't prove it — armadillos and raccoons also dig for earthworms. Pulling back a patch of turf to count grubs confirms it; a lawn technician can check density and treat if it's over threshold.
copy.fact: This covers Phyllophaga species (the classic 'June bug' larva) plus several other scarab beetle larvae that look nearly identical underground.
copy.blurb: Animal digging at night is often the first clue. Pulling back the turf to count grubs confirms it.

tech_notes: Tug test — roots sheared at grub-damaged spots. Cut-and-peel count per sq ft; treat over threshold per label, water-in required.

traits: Chalk-white to gray weevil with a short snout, about 6-8.5 mm
Leaf edges notched inward from the margin like pinking shears
Drops and plays dead when the branch is bumped
Feeds on a very wide range of ornamentals — over 150 plant species

look_alikes.difference: Sri Lankan weevil is chalky white to gray with a short snout; Diaprepes root weevil has a black wing cover banded with orange or yellow.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up from above showing the wing-cover color pattern, next to a coin.

copy.what_it_means: A newer Florida arrival that already feeds on more than 150 plant species — the notched-leaf signature turns up almost everywhere. Cosmetic on mature plants; young or newly planted ornamentals can need protection.
copy.fact: A newer Florida arrival that already feeds on 150+ plant species — the notched-leaf signature is everywhere.
copy.blurb: Cosmetic on mature plants; young ornamentals may need protection.

tech_notes: Confirm leaf-margin notching + play-dead drop behavior. Weevils fly/hide readily, limiting contact-spray success; targeted ornamental treatment on high-value plants.

traits: Round, domed body about the size of a small pea, orange to red with 0 to 19 black spots
A black marking shaped like an 'M' or 'W' sits just behind the head
Shows up by the dozens or hundreds on sunny walls or squeezes indoors during cool fronts
Releases a yellow, foul-smelling fluid that can stain when crushed or handled

look_alikes.difference: Asian lady beetle has a black 'M' or 'W' mark behind the head; native lady beetles lack that marking
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in looking straight down at the head and the area just behind it.

look_alikes.difference: Mealybug destroyer adults are solid black with an orange-tan head and tail patch and have no spots at all
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in from directly above showing the whole back, checking for spots vs. solid black.

safety_line: Can give a light pinch-bite and its yellow defense fluid stains fabric; large indoor clusters occasionally bother people with allergies or asthma.

copy.what_it_means: A beneficial aphid-eater that becomes a nuisance when cool fronts push it indoors by the dozens to overwinter. It doesn't damage homes or belongings, but large clusters and their staining defense fluid can be unpleasant to live with.
copy.fact: It was brought to the US on purpose decades ago to eat crop aphids, and it still does that job well outdoors most of the year.

tech_notes: Confirm the black M/W marking behind the head and color-morph variability to rule out native Coccinellidae. Exterior perimeter treatment around entry points reduces indoor invasion; avoid interior application near food/aggregation sites.

review.notes: Re-read UF/IFAS EDIS IN361/EENY204 (Mizell) directly and confirmed: overwintering movement indoors happens progressively later moving south (October in Michigan, November-January in north Florida); the document never separately characterizes south/southwest Florida's aggregation frequency. Range stays 'occasional' and peak_months (Dec-Feb) is used only as a reasonable extension of that same documented north-to-south gradient further south -- neither is claimed as a confirmed SWFL figure. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Small, domed, oval beetle, usually red, orange or yellow with black spots (pattern varies by species)
No black 'M'/'W' marking behind the head the way an Asian lady beetle has
Found on leaves and stems with aphids nearby, rather than swarming walls or windows
Larvae are spiky, alligator-shaped, and gray or black with orange markings, also hunting aphids

look_alikes.difference: Native lady beetles lack the black 'M'/'W' mark behind the head, and don't gather indoors by the hundreds
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in looking straight down at the head and the area just behind it.

copy.what_it_means: A garden ally that eats aphids and other soft-bodied plant pests. Seeing them on your plants is a good sign, not a pest problem, and they're worth leaving alone.
copy.fact: A single lady beetle can eat thousands of aphids over its lifetime, larva and adult stage combined.

tech_notes: Confirm absence of the black M/W head marking and lack of large indoor aggregations to rule out Harmonia axyridis. No treatment indicated; flag as beneficial if seen during an inspection.

review.notes: Entry covers Florida's many native lady beetle species collectively (rank family); appearance varies a lot by species, so traits describe the general pattern rather than one look. Generic ladybug/ladybird names resolve to the shared lady-beetles subgroup; this entry requires a native qualifier. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Adult is solid black with an orange-tan head and rear wing-tip patch, no spots at all
Larvae are covered in long white waxy filaments and look bigger and fuzzier than the mealybugs nearby
Found moving through mealybug colonies on stems, leaf axils and citrus twigs
Larvae move noticeably faster than the slow, stationary mealybugs they're feeding on

look_alikes.difference: Destroyer larvae are larger, move quickly, and have longer waxy filaments; mealybugs are slower, smaller, and stay clustered in place
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of one insect actually walking, showing its speed and the length of its waxy strands

look_alikes.difference: Mealybug destroyer adults are solid black with an orange-tan head/tail and have no spots; Asian lady beetles are orange or red with black spots
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in from directly above showing the whole back, checking for spots vs. solid black.

copy.what_it_means: A predatory beetle that feeds specifically on mealybugs, larva and adult alike. Finding it on a mealybug-infested plant is a good sign the pest population is already being knocked back naturally.
copy.fact: Its larvae disguise themselves in white wax so well that they're often mistaken for the very mealybugs they're eating.

tech_notes: Confirm larva speed and filament length against static mealybug colonies before recommending any treatment; avoid broad-spectrum sprays on plants hosting active destroyer populations.

review.notes: Range in SWFL marked occasional; it's naturally present and also released commercially, but homeowners rarely notice or report it, so confidence is moderate. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Chunky, oval, shiny beetle about 1/2 to 1 inch long, tan to reddish-brown or black
Bangs repeatedly against porch lights, windows and screens on warm nights
Smooth, rounded back with no horns, spots or eyespots
Larvae are fat, white, C-shaped grubs found in the soil under thinning or dying lawn

look_alikes.difference: Ox beetle males have three long curved horns on the head and front of the back; June beetles have a smooth, hornless back
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo from the side showing the head and the front of the back for horns

copy.what_it_means: The clumsy beetle that thumps into porch lights on spring evenings is basically harmless. Its grub stage (a white grub in the soil) is the one worth watching, since heavy grub numbers can thin out lawn roots and cause dead patches.
copy.fact: There are well over 100 Phyllophaga species in Florida, which is why 'June beetle' really covers a whole group rather than just one insect.

tech_notes: Confirm white C-shaped grubs in soil samples under damaged turf before treating; adult flights to light are not themselves treatment triggers.

review.notes: Entry covers the Phyllophaga genus as a group (common name 'June/May beetle'); exact species present in SWFL vary and weren't individually confirmed.

traits: Large, heavy-bodied black to dark brown beetle, often over 1 inch long
Males have three curved horns on the head and front of the back; females are hornless with small bumps instead
Found on the ground near outdoor lights or in mulch/soil, moves slowly
Doesn't bite, sting or fly at people despite its intimidating size

look_alikes.difference: June beetles are smaller and completely hornless with a smooth back; ox beetle males carry three curved horns
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo from the side showing the head and front of the back for horns

look_alikes.difference: Eyed click beetle has two large false eyespots on its back and clicks itself upright when flipped; ox beetle has horns and no eyespots or click
look_alikes.next_photo: A top-down close-up of the area just behind the head, plus flip the beetle to see if it clicks

copy.what_it_means: An impressively large but harmless beetle. Its grubs live in decaying wood, mulch and compost and aren't a threat to a healthy lawn or garden, so this one is a look-don't-treat situation.
copy.fact: Males use their curved horns to wrestle rival males, more like tiny bulls than biting insects.

tech_notes: No treatment indicated; reassure on size/horns, this genus does not damage living plants or structures in a way that warrants control.

review.notes: Re-checked UF/IFAS EDIS IN759 directly this session: it covers appearance, horns and handling but gives no Florida regional frequency or abundance data for Strategus species at all -- not even statewide. Range is kept at 'occasional', this catalog's standard cautious default when no frequency source exists, rather than asserted as a confirmed figure. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Large, elongated, mottled black-and-white beetle, often 1 to 1.75 inches long
Two big black false eyespots ringed in white sit on the back of the beetle, just behind the head
Flips itself upright with an audible click if placed or found on its back
Found on tree bark, firewood piles and rotting logs, especially near hardwoods

look_alikes.difference: Eyed click beetle has two large false eyespots behind the head and clicks when flipped; ox beetle has horns instead of eyespots and does not click
look_alikes.next_photo: A top-down close-up of the area just behind the head, plus flip the beetle to see if it clicks

copy.what_it_means: A harmless, even helpful beetle whose fake 'eyes' are just a bluff to startle predators. Its larvae hunt other wood-boring insect grubs in rotting logs, so it's a natural check on those pests, not a pest itself.
copy.fact: Its clicking trick is actually a spring-loaded mechanism it uses to flip itself right-side up if it lands on its back.

tech_notes: No treatment indicated; beneficial predator of wood-boring larvae. Reassure on size and eyespots.

review.notes: Re-fetched UF/IFAS EDIS IN242 directly this session: it confirms the species occurs in Florida and documents a real late-May Florida collection record, though not a peak-month range. peak_months (May-Jul) anchors on that Florida record, broadly corroborated (not confirmed) by a general, non-Florida-specific source (Animal Diversity Web) describing June-July adult abundance. No SWFL-specific data exists, but this is the best Florida-anchored basis available, so season_basis moves from 'unverified' to 'observed' rather than being left fully unresolved. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Large, shiny black beetle over 1 inch long with deeply grooved, ridged wing covers
A single small curved horn on the head
Found in groups tunneling inside rotting logs and stumps, not in dry structural wood
Makes an audible squeaking or hissing sound when picked up or handled

look_alikes.difference: Bess beetle has hard, deeply grooved wing covers and one head horn; Florida woods roach has a smooth, unridged shell and no horn
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in looking straight down at the back, checking for grooves/ridges vs. a smooth shell.

copy.what_it_means: A wood decomposer, not a wood destroyer. It only works on already-rotting logs and stumps and has no interest in sound lumber or living trees, so finding one in a mulch pile or old firewood is nothing to worry about.
copy.fact: Bess beetles live in small family groups inside their log and actually communicate with each other using at least 14 distinct squeaking sounds.

tech_notes: No treatment indicated; if found near a structure, confirm it's associated with decaying wood/mulch, not sound structural timber, to distinguish from a wood-destroying pest inquiry.

traits: Shiny black or dark metallic beetle, fast-moving on long legs
Narrow head with prominent jaws, no horns, no colorful spots
Found scurrying under stones, mulch, pots or logs, usually after dark
Runs to hide rather than fly when a light or hand disturbs it

look_alikes.difference: Ground beetles have hard wing covers meeting in a straight line; cockroaches have softer, overlapping wings and longer antennae
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in from above on the back and the antennae length.

safety_line: Its jaws can pinch if it's picked up, but this isn't a beetle that bites people unprovoked.

copy.what_it_means: A fast-moving nighttime predator that eats caterpillars, slugs and other garden pests. Seeing one scurry under a pot or mulch is a good sign for your garden, not a reason for concern.
copy.fact: Some ground beetles can outrun almost anything else their size, covering many times their own body length per second.

tech_notes: No treatment indicated; beneficial predator. Distinguish from small roach species if the report is from indoors. Per BRIEF Revision 3 rule 5, safety.bites is true as a capability flag (prominent jaws can pinch if handled).

review.notes: Generic family-level entry; Florida hosts many ground beetle species with varied size/color, so traits describe the common pattern homeowners see rather than one species. Per audit item 44: safety.bites changed from false to true (capability, not danger, per rule 5); risk changed from low to defensive to match. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Tiny (under 1/4 inch), narrow, reddish-brown to dark brown beetle
Round exit holes about 1/16 to 1/8 inch across scattered over bare or finished wood
Fine, flour-like powder packed tightly inside the wood and sifting out of the holes
Found in untreated hardwood furniture, flooring, moldings or lumber, not in soil-contact wood

look_alikes.difference: Powderpost powder is fine and packed tight behind small round holes; termite pellets are loose, hard pellets pushed out separate 'kick-out' holes
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the hole and the loose material beneath it, next to a coin for scale

safety_line: No risk to people or pets; the concern is only for untreated hardwood furniture, flooring and structural lumber.

copy.what_it_means: A small beetle that can quietly hollow out hardwood furniture, flooring or lumber over months to years, leaving pinholes and fine powder behind. It's worth an inspection to confirm which wood-boring insect is active and whether it's still emerging.
copy.fact: Powderpost beetles can re-infest the same piece of wood for generations, since females often lay eggs right back into old exit holes.

tech_notes: Confirm active infestation (fresh, light-colored frass and clean-edged holes) vs. old, inactive damage before recommending treatment. Distinguish Lyctinae frass/hole size from Bostrichidae and drywood termite pellets per label references.

traits: Small oval weevil, black body overlaid with a mottled pattern of white, yellow, orange or red scales
Distinctive squared-off notches chewed from the edges of young leaves in a scalloped pattern
Found on citrus and ornamental leaves, especially after rain, no long curved snout
Legless white larvae feed unseen on roots below ground, causing decline that shows up above ground later

look_alikes.difference: Diaprepes weevil is small and mottled, feeding on citrus/ornamental leaves; palmetto weevil is much larger, plain black-to-red, on palms only
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up next to a coin showing size and color pattern, plus a photo of what plant it's on

safety_line: Florida regulates this pest under nursery/citrus quarantine rules; a suspected find on nursery stock should be reported rather than moved off-site.

copy.what_it_means: The leaf notching is only half the story; the damage that really hurts citrus and ornamentals happens underground, where the larvae chew on roots for months. Leaf notching on a valued tree or shrub is worth a look before root damage adds up.
copy.fact: A single female can lay thousands of eggs in her lifetime, folded and glued inside pairs of leaves.

tech_notes: Confirm adult scale-pattern and leaf notching, then inspect root zone/soil for larvae and decline symptoms; multiple overlapping generations are typical in Florida's climate.

review.notes: regulated confirmed true: Florida Administrative Code 5B-3.0038 (Quarantine Action) lists Diaprepes abbreviatus as a Florida plant pest of limited distribution, subject to immediate quarantine of infested nursery stock. safety_line added accordingly.

traits: Largest weevil in North America, adults 3/4 to 1.2 inches long, black to reddish with a long curved snout
Found on stressed, wounded or recently transplanted palms, especially cabbage palm
Newest leaves in the crown wilt and droop first, then the whole top of the palm can collapse ('popped neck')
Larvae are large, legless, cream-colored grubs found inside the trunk or crown when a palm is cut open

look_alikes.difference: South American palm weevil runs larger and darker with an even longer snout; both attack palm crowns, so size and snout length matter more than color alone
look_alikes.next_photo: A side-on close-up of the weevil next to a coin, plus a photo of the palm species it was found on

look_alikes.difference: Palmetto weevil is much larger and found only on palms; diaprepes root weevil is small, mottled, and feeds on citrus/ornamental leaves, not palm crowns
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up next to a coin showing size and color pattern, plus a photo of what plant it's on

look_alikes.difference: Palmetto weevil grubs kill the growing point and the whole crown can collapse ("popped neck"); royal palm bug only scars new fronds cosmetically.
look_alikes.next_photo: A wide shot of the whole crown: drooping/collapsing older fronds and a wilting or fallen crown (weevil) versus frizzled new fronds only (bug).

copy.what_it_means: This native weevil targets palms that are already stressed, wounded or freshly transplanted, and by the time the crown visibly droops the damage inside is often already done. A recently transplanted or storm-damaged palm showing crown wilt is worth a prompt look.
copy.fact: Despite being North America's largest weevil, it's native to Florida and mostly goes after palms that are already struggling rather than healthy ones.

tech_notes: Confirm crown symptoms (wilting newest fronds, 'popped neck') and check for grubs/frass in the crown or trunk; recent transplant or storm/pruning wounds are the key risk factor to note.

review.notes: Peak months set to hurricane/storm season when transplanting and wind damage stress palms; not a directly cited seasonal-activity figure. Per audit item 54: added a reciprocal look-alike to royal-palm-bug (B/true-bugs) since UF/IFAS EDIS IN139 documents royal palm as a host, and the cosmetic-vs-potentially-fatal distinction is useful triage information.

traits: Very large weevil, often 1.5 to 2 inches long, black with a long, downward-curved snout
Found boring into the crown of palms, especially date, coconut and Canary Island date palms
Palm crown collapses ('popped neck') and fronds droop and die from the top down
Larger overall than the native palmetto weevil, with an even longer snout

look_alikes.difference: Palmetto weevil is native, somewhat smaller, black-to-red; South American palm weevil runs larger, more uniformly dark, with a longer snout
look_alikes.next_photo: A side-on close-up of the weevil next to a coin, plus a photo of the palm species it was found on

safety_line: This is a regulated pest of concern for Florida palms; note where you saw it and avoid moving cut palm material off-site while it's confirmed.

copy.what_it_means: A large palm-killing weevil not yet known to be established in Florida, monitored closely because of how much damage it does elsewhere and how easily it can spread in palm material. A suspected find on a declining palm is worth a professional look and a report so the sighting can be tracked.
copy.fact: It can also carry a nematode that causes red-ring disease in coconut and oil palms, adding a second way it harms palms beyond direct feeding.

tech_notes: Confirm size and snout length against native palmetto weevil; if suspected, photograph in place, avoid moving material, and follow current agency reporting guidance for this species of concern.

review.notes: Both verification items resolved this session. Established/present in FL: not established — EDDMapS shows no Florida point data (checked live), the EPPO datasheet (gd.eppo.int/taxon/RHYCPA) documents established US populations only in California (since 2015), Texas and Arizona (trapped adults, no established population as of 2020), and the 2010 FDACS pest alert (DACS-P-01719) lists it only as a threat, not present. Regulated status: confirmed regulated — Florida Administrative Code 5B-65.003 (Wood Boring Pests, Wood Inhabiting Pests, and Plant Pests) explicitly lists 'Rhynchophorus palmarum, American palm weevil' as a regulated pest; safety.regulated changed back to true and safety_line updated accordingly. range/action/referral (rare, report, report_fdacs) already matched a not-yet-established, regulated species of concern, so left as-is.

traits: Small (under 1/2 inch) dark brown to black weevil with a short curved snout
Often seen walking on sidewalks or driveways near the lawn rather than flying
Sawdust-like frass packed tightly inside chewed grass stems near the soil line
Damaged zoysia or bermuda grass pulls up easily in irregular, spreading dead patches

look_alikes.difference: Billbug is a small weevil with a curved snout, seen on pavement; mole cricket is much larger with shovel-like front legs, stays in soil
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up next to a coin showing either the weevil's snout or the cricket's shovel-shaped front legs

copy.what_it_means: This weevil chews through grass stems at the base, and by the time patches of turf pull up easily by hand, both adults and larvae are usually already at work below. Spreading irregular dead patches in zoysia or bermuda grass are worth a lawn inspection.
copy.fact: A quick way to check is the 'tug test': damaged grass in a billbug patch pulls free from the soil with almost no resistance.

tech_notes: Confirm with tug test and look for sawdust-like frass in stems plus legless larvae in the top two inches of soil; damage often misread as drought or dormancy stress.

review.notes: Returned to draft after removing the generic 'billbug' and 'billbugs' aliases, which cannot identify this hunting billbug subspecies; owner re-approval is required. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Small, flattened, disc- or shield-shaped beetle with edges that flare out past its legs
Often shiny gold, green or amber, and some can shift color when disturbed
Found feeding on morning glory, sweet potato or other related vine leaves
Leaves show small round or irregular chewed holes rather than notched edges

look_alikes.difference: Tortoise beetle is flat with edges flaring past its legs like a shield; lady beetles are domed, curving straight down to the legs
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up from the side showing whether the edges flare out flat or curve down to meet the legs

copy.what_it_means: A small, oddly shield-shaped beetle that nibbles holes in morning glory and sweet potato leaves. The feeding is usually light and cosmetic, so it's mostly a matter of keeping an eye on numbers rather than treating.
copy.fact: Some tortoise beetles can shift color when they're handled or disturbed, going from shiny gold to a duller shade in seconds.

tech_notes: No treatment usually needed at low numbers; monitor host vines (morning glory/sweet potato family) if leaf damage is spreading.

review.notes: Generic subfamily-level entry; several tortoise beetle species occur in Florida with varying color, so traits describe the common shield shape rather than one exact species.

traits: Toothpick-like columns of frass pushing out of the bark, or white sugary crust around small holes
Small round entry holes in the bark, often no bigger than a pinhead
Branch dieback or a declining tree, often one that was already stressed
Beetles are tiny and usually not seen; the frass and holes are the clue

look_alikes.difference: Powderpost beetles work dry, seasoned wood and leave fine powder; shot-hole borers and ambrosia beetles attack living or stressed trees and leave frass columns.
look_alikes.next_photo: A wide shot showing whether the holes are in a living tree or in finished wood, then a close-up of the frass.

look_alikes.difference: Drywood termite pellets are tiny, uniform and pile up under wood; borer frass pushes out of bark as thin, toothpick-like columns or a sugary crust.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the frass shape and where it is coming from, tree bark or structural wood.

copy.what_it_means: Toothpick-like frass or a sugary crust around small holes in bark, with branch dieback, can suggest shot-hole borers or ambrosia beetles. A photo cannot identify the beetle; an arborist looks at what stressed the tree and whether it is worth saving.
copy.fact: Ambrosia beetles farm a fungus inside the wood as food, and most kinds go after trees that are already stressed or dying.

tech_notes: Find the small entry holes and frass columns; look for whatever stressed the tree (flooding, drought, wounds, root problems). Invasive shot-hole borers can also attack apparently healthy trees, so refer to an arborist rather than a routine service visit.

review.notes: Draft for owner catalog review (2026-09-30 yard-rotation species set). Placed in beetles/weevils (Scolytinae is a subfamily of Curculionidae) as a group-level entry, not a single species. Service line is tree_shrub with an arborist referral instead of line none: the v1-map test requires any pest-section entry with line none to sit in an all-none group, and beetles is mixed. FR422 page could not be read directly (see verification).

verification.note: From the owner brief. The FR422 page returned HTTP 410 to the fetch tool; a UF/IFAS search result confirms the title (Diagnosis and Management of the Invasive Shot Hole Borers) and the white sugary "volcano" sign on avocado, but the frass description was not read from the page.

symptoms: Toothpick-like columns of frass pushing out of the bark, or white sugary crust around small holes
Small round entry holes in the bark, often no bigger than a pinhead

required_signature.text: No photo confirms shot-hole or ambrosia beetles. A technician or arborist checks the entry holes and frass on the tree.
elements: Toothpick-like columns of frass pushing out of the bark, or white sugary crust around small holes

differentials.difference: Powderpost beetles work dry, seasoned wood and leave fine powder; shot-hole borers and ambrosia beetles attack living or stressed trees and leave frass columns.
differentials.next_observation: A technician checks this on site.

differentials.difference: Drywood termite pellets are tiny, uniform and pile up under wood; borer frass pushes out of bark as thin, toothpick-like columns or a sugary crust.
differentials.next_observation: A technician checks this on site.

condition.recovery_note: Whether the tree recovers depends on how stressed it was; an arborist judges the tree.
